content.overview: Outbreak scope is reconstructed from compatible evidence: plant/lot identity, timestamps, scouting denominators, spatial pattern, movement history, shared tools/water/environment and testing. A convenient observation is not enough to define the whole affected population.

vocabulary.definition: The plants, lots, rooms, materials or processes reasonably included in the event based on evidence.
The time period during which material or areas may have encountered the suspected source or pathway.
A map of linked plants, tools, people, water systems, rooms or materials that could connect the source to downstream exposure.

sections.title: Start with identity and time
sections.body: Plant/lot genealogy, movement timestamps and task records narrow the population that could plausibly share exposure. Preserve uncertainty when records are incomplete.

sections.title: Use spatial pattern and denominators
sections.body: Clustered, edge-associated, irrigation-zone and room-wide patterns support different pathway hypotheses. Scouting denominator and route are necessary to interpret apparent prevalence.

sections.title: Test pathway hypotheses against evidence
sections.body: Compare movement, environmental, root-zone, propagation and sanitation records with the observed distribution rather than accepting the first plausible story.

workedExamples: If all affected plants came from one donor but share no unique room location, propagation lineage may deserve higher priority than an HVAC-only hypothesis.
commonMistakes: Defining affected scope as the entire facility without evidence.
Using a positive result without preserving sample identity.
content.practicalApplication: Create an outbreak map with confirmed affected units, possible exposures, unaffected comparators, shared pathways and evidence gaps.
content.summary: Affected scope is an evidence reconstruction problem. Identity, time, distribution and pathways must agree before broad conclusions are justified.
